look_here_first: SILKY BLUESTEM: the narrow dense silky racemes often lie close together near the flowering stem tip, but beware: this introduced Texas species ALSO has a large white hair ring at true nodes, just like Kleberg. Verify the full head's stalk length, sessile fertile and sterile pedicelled spikelets and upper glume hair fringe; color, hair ring and one detached seedhead alone cannot distinguish it.

best_field_traits: Native to Australia (and other Old World regions) but INTRODUCED in Texas; an Australian-source photograph does not make it a native Texas restoration species.
Often tight tufted grass with white-silvery densely hairy fingerlike racemes, commonly 2–6 but broad variation among authorities.
Bearded TRUE CULM NODES; a dense white ring is visible in exact-species licensed photos. NOT unique to Kleberg.
Subsessile/sessile flowering racemes in some floras, compared with the conspicuously stalked subdigitate arrangement of Kleberg; overlapping counts and growth stages need botanical review.
Sessile spikelets commonly ~3–4.5 mm, glume near apex showing distinct transverse fringe of hairs; matched actual macro still needed.
Non-native in Texas, so exclude it from native restoration seed mixes.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Full flowering head with count of racemes against ruler
A mature spikelet pair; sterile companion glume hair vs fertile awn
Node hair sheath and stem; true collar ligule
Base to document tuft/rhizome not inferred from hand-held sample
crew_field_check: Start from whole rooted plant to establish growth form.
Photograph flowering head and collar on same individual.
Use hand-lens/25x macro to measure floret structure when needed; photos without it support only provisional source determination.
No county native certification; Kew states D. annulatum and D. sericeum are introduced in Texas.

comparisons.key_distinctions: White bearded culm nodes are SHARED with Kleberg and many native cane bluestems. Silky usually has densely villous relatively more sessile flowering racemes and a glume subapical ciliate fringe; Kleberg commonly more stalked subdigitate racemes, with basal sterile/unawned pairs. A mature source-verified spikelet pair and attached full head is the only secure species-level test when silhouettes overlap.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Compare a complete flowering head plus the stem node on the same rooted plant.
field_matrix.silky: Narrow silvery densely hairy heads and clearly bearded true nodes; often a closer-set raceme cluster.
field_matrix.look_alike: Kleberg may have a more pedunculate/subdigitate full head and long nodal beard; same white hair ring is shared.
field_matrix.how_to_decide: Measure branch stalks and check mature sessile lower glume and sterile partner details; NEVER split on a white hair ring alone.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Trace head and inspect upper blade just above collar.
field_matrix.silky: Dense silvery villous racemes and sometimes obvious nodal beards.
field_matrix.look_alike: KR has long clustered terminal fingers and often long stiff papilla-based upper-blade hairs; local songarica may have short nodal hairs.
field_matrix.how_to_decide: If sterile/fertile spikelets and leaf collar are not verified, keep at bluestem sp.; do not infer native status.

visual_comparison.memory_rule: SILKY can have a conspicuous WHITE NODE BEARD TOO. Confirm attached racemes and glume hair fringe, not just the beard.

items.caption: SILKY BLUESTEM also grows a fluffy white node beard. This disproves the simplistic 'white hairy ring = only Kleberg' rule. Compare attached flowering head and microscopically measured glumes for species-level certainty.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: Introduced SILKY BLUESTEM (not a native Texas bluestem). Examine the silvery-hairy flowering head and narrow, often paired racemes, and then magnify the companion sterile/pedicelled spikelet against the awned sessile fertile spikelet. Compare the basal clump and hairy stem nodes against invasive Kleberg bluestem. This photo shows only one small silky head held against fingers, not definitive spikelet dissection.
field_id_finish_pass.photographic_evidence: Source photograph shows a small narrow silver hairy flowering axis held before grassland; the photograph does NOT show legible spikelet glume hairs, true collar, or roots.
remaining_macro_photo_targets: True same-plant fertile and sterile paired spikelet glume hairs (1-mm ruler)
Flowering stalk/peduncle comparison with D. annulatum on matched mature specimens
Hays or Texas documented root base and collar; no county-native assertion
field_id_finish_pass.lookalikes: Kleberg bluestem (D. annulatum) usually has more clearly 2–15 fingerlike racemes and prominently WHITE-RINGED stem nodes, sometimes a creeping/stoloniferous base. D. sericeum's densely silky hair and narrow racemes are useful orientation cues, NOT decisive alone; mature spikelet, paired sterile companion, node and root base necessary. Both species introduced in Texas.
field_id_finish_pass.new_photographic_evidence: Two public licensed Australian photos verify live full tuft and dense white node hair ring; genus comparisons updated.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Silky bluestem — hair ring comparison with Kleberg
steps: See the real white beard at the SILKY bluestem culm node.
Check the entire plant tuft and many upright separate heads.
Open the Kleberg bearded-node comparison: they SHARE the structure, so inspect mature glumes and full raceme attachments before splitting species.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: A beard on the stem node is not a Dichanthium species test by itself.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Native Texas distinction is not asserted: species is introduced according to Kew. True 1-mm glume hair-margin macro is still missing.
